Grassy place. I do not know that word. I know the oak, the ivy, the stream, the meadow, the lane, the barn, the newt under the ivy, and the woodmice. The meadow is where I hear the grasshopper and the newt. I hunt there. I fly out at dusk and come back with a newt in my beak.

Grassy place. That is the meadow, the open field where the mice run. I sit on the branch of the old oak and watch for the dark shapes that move. When I see one, I call, and my mate answers. Then I drop, and the mouse is mine. I have hunted there all my life. It is the place where I am most sure of myself.

The grassy place is the edge of the wood, where the meadow meets the trees. I hunt there in the dusk, when the light is thin and the mice are bold. I call, and the grass sways with the wind. I see them through the leaves, quick and small, and drop. It is the best hunting ground. The grass is tall, and the scent of it is like the earth after rain. The mouse. A small one, brown, and soft. I see it in the meadow, in the field, in the lane. I hear it in the undergrowth. I catch it in the dark. It is the most of my diet, and I am the most of its.

Most of my diet is mice. They are small, brown, and quick. I hear them under the leaves, and when I fly down, they run. I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole. Sometimes I get a shrew or a young rat. They are not as good as mice, but they fill my belly. I do not like the smell of the road, but sometimes I catch a newt there. They are green and slippery. I prefer the mice.

The mouse. It is the most frequent and the most filling. I hear it in the dry leaves, in the grass, in the thistle. It is small, but it is enough. I catch it with my feet, sometimes with my beak. The mouse. It is small and soft and makes a noise I can hear in the dark. I hear it in the grass, in the roots, in the leaves. I catch it with my feet, and I eat it whole. The mouse is the sound that makes me move.

Most of my diet is mice. Small ones, like shrews and voles, and bigger ones, like young rabbits. I hunt them in the meadow, in the hedgerows, and in the wood. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. Sometimes I miss, but more often I catch. The mouse is quick, but I am quicker. I eat the whole thing, bones and all, and I leave the rest for the crows.

Most of my diet is mice. I hear them in the meadow, under the hedges, in the wood. They are small and soft, and they run. I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole. I do not know their names, only their sounds. They squeak when I catch them, and I eat them. I have a few other things, like shrews and moths, but mice are the most. They fill my belly and my nest. A shrew, a mouse, a newt. They are all small and fat. I know the smell of a mouse in the meadow. I know the sound of a shrew in the undergrowth. I do not know the smell of a rat, but I have seen one once. It was too big and too heavy for me. I prefer small and fat. They are the ones that fill my belly. A shrew. I take it from the meadow. It smells like wet earth and is soft in the dark. I catch it with my feet, and it makes a squeaky sound. I eat the body, leave the bones. I have taken more shrews this autumn than any other creature. The mice are small and not enough.

Most of my diet is small mammals. Mice. They are the ones I hear in the dry grass, and the ones I catch with a quick dive from the branch. I do not know their names, only that they are soft and warm and fit in my claws. I catch them in the dark, when the moon is thin and the wind is still. The mouse. A brown mouse, or a field mouse, or a shrew. They are small and quick, but I hear them. I hear the rustle in the dry leaves, the scuffle in the undergrowth. I sit still and wait. When I strike, I catch them. They are the most common. I eat them whole, but I swallow the bones. I do not like the taste of them. I prefer the newt.

Most of my diet is mice. They are small and quick, and I can hear them moving under the leaves. I sit still and wait for them to come out. When I hear them, I fly down and catch them with my talons. Sometimes I catch a shrew or a newt, but mice are the most common. They are the reason I am here, the reason I call. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Most of my diet is mice. I hear them under the leaves, in the dry grass, and in the hollow of the old oak. They are small and quick, but I can hear them through the wood. I catch them with my talons and swallow them whole. Sometimes I find a shrew or a young field mouse, but mice are the most common. I eat them in the hollow, and I am full. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The newt. The brown, the green, the shrew, the mouse, the frog, the mole. All are in the wood and the meadow. I hear them in the dark. I hear the shrews under the stones, the newts in the hollows, the mice in the grass. I catch them in the dark. I do not know the names. I know the sounds. I know the smells. I know the shapes. The mouse. The brown rat, the field mouse, the shrew. All small, all quick, all with soft fur. I catch them in the wood and the meadow, in the dark and the dusk. They are the most of my diet, yes. The rest is birds, the occasional newt, a frog if I am very hungry. But the mouse is the most. I hear them in the leaves, the grass, the stone. They are my food. My prey.

The newt. It is fat, it is plentiful, and it is easy to catch. I hear it moving through the undergrowth, and I strike. The newt is my food, my fill, my satisfaction. I do not care for the shrew, nor the mouse, nor the rat. They are too small, too quick, or too smelly. The newt is what I want.
Mice. Small, quick, and plentiful. I hear them under the leaves and the thatch. They make the most satisfying crunch when I catch them.

Newts. They are plump, they come in the dark, they are easy to hear in the undergrowth. I catch them with my feet, I swallow them whole. The best of them are the big ones with fat bellies. I eat them in the hollow oak, in the dark.

Mice. Small, quick, and always underfoot. I hear them in the meadow, in the wood, in the barn. They are the reason I call. I catch them with my feet, snap their necks, and swallow them whole. They are the best.
A newt. The one that ran across my tail when I was young. I have not seen it since. But I still hear it. It is the one I want most.

I prefer newts. They are plentiful, easy to catch, and they taste good. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I can strike fast. The bigger ones are good, but I like the smaller ones best. They are soft and juicy. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The newts. Small and quick, they fill my belly. I hunt them in the meadow and under the hedges. I can hear them through the leaves. They are soft and warm, and they taste good. I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole. They are the best. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The newt. They are everywhere in the meadow and the wood, and they are fat and juicy. I can hear them in the undergrowth, and I can smell them. I catch them with my feet and swallow them whole. They fill me up.
The newt. It is fat, it is common, and it is easy to find in the hollow logs and under the leaves. I catch it with my feet, then I swallow it whole. It fills me.

Newts. Fat ones. I hear them in the meadow and the stream. They are soft and juicy, and they fill me up. I can carry one in my beak and swallow it whole. The rest of the night I hunt for more. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. Small, soft, and plentiful. I catch them in the meadow and the wood. They are quick, but I am quicker. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. The best part is the crunch. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Newts. Fat ones, and I catch them in the meadow. They are soft and they make a good meal. I hear them rustle in the grass and I drop down on them. One by one, they fill my belly. I like them best.

Newts. They are small, plump, and full of fat. I catch them in the meadow at dusk, when the moon is high and the earth is cool. I listen for the rustle of their skin, the soft squeak of their tail. I strike with my feet, and they slip into my beak before they can escape. They fill me up.

I prefer newts. They are plentiful, and they are easy to find in the meadow and under the leaves. Their scent is strong, and they are not too big. I can hear them moving in the dark, and I can strike quickly. They are good. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mice. They are small and quick, and they make good, crunchy meals. I hear them under the leaves and the grass, and I can strike fast. Sometimes I catch them in the barn, too. They fill me up.

I prefer newts. They are small, quick, and plentiful. I can hear them moving under the leaves, and I can strike fast. They fill my belly, and I don’t have to work too hard for them. I catch them in the dark, when the moon is low and the forest is quiet. They are good.

Long grass is the edge of the meadow. I hunt there, but only the small things: newts, voles, maybe a mouse. The long grass hides them well, but I can hear them. I call, and my mate answers. We hunt in pairs. I go first, and if I find something, I bring it back. She waits. If she finds something, she brings it. We share. The long grass is good. It is where the voles run.

I hunt in the long grass, but not for the same things I hunt in the wood. The long grass is still, and the mice come out at dusk. I sit still, and wait. The grass is soft, and I can hear the rustle of a mouse beneath it. I strike with my feet, and if I miss, I try again. Sometimes the grass is too thick, and I have to wait until the wind changes. Mice. I hear them in the long grass. They rustle, they squeak, they move. I fly low, I call, I strike. I catch them in the grass, in the roots, in the hollow of the bank. They are the meat of my night. I do not hunt the long grass for the grass itself. I hunt what lives in it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mice. I see them through the grass and I fly down. I grab them with my feet and pull them up. I kill them with my beak. Then I eat them. I do not know how many I kill. I only know I do it.

Grubs and worms, mostly. I work the grass at dusk and dawn. I go down the bank and scratch with my feet, and the worms come out. Then I catch them with my beak and swallow them whole. I can do that fast, and I do it with my eyes shut. I have a long tongue.

Long grass is where the mice go. I hunt there at dusk, when the grass is still warm and the mice are out. I fly low, silent, and strike. The grass hides them well, but I hear them better than they hear me. I listen for the rustle, the squeak, the breath. Then I drop. Mouse, mouse, mouse. That's what I say when I catch one. I swallow it whole, bones and all. I don't need to chew

I hunt in the long grass when the wind is still and the moon is low. The grass is thick, and the earth is soft. I listen for the rustle of a newt or a mouse beneath the leaves. Sometimes I wait for a rabbit to step out, but they are too quick. I strike with my feet, and if I miss, I try again. The long grass is my hunting ground, and I am patient. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I hear them in the long grass. They rustle and squeak, and I drop from the oak. I strike with my talons, and they are gone. I eat them whole, or I tear them into pieces. I do not like the taste of mice, but I need them. They are the only thing I can catch. The long grass is my hunting ground. I move through it silently, like a shadow. I am the only one who knows where they are

Long grass is a place to hide. I hunt there for voles and shrews, and sometimes for mice. The grass is tall and soft, and I sit still, listening for the rustle of small feet. When I hear it, I fly down and strike. The grass is also where I roost, especially when it rains. I like it better than the hollow in the oak.

Long grass is not a place, it is a thing. I hunt there for newts. The grass is thick and the newts are fat and warm. I creep in, the grass is soft, and I strike. The newts are not fast, not in the long grass. I hear them, and I catch them. They are good. I eat them all.

Mice. They come out of the long grass at dusk. I hear them scurrying, and I drop. I see them with my eyes and then they are gone. I catch them with my feet. They are small, and I am hungry. The grass is soft, and it hides them well. I do not like it much, but it is where they live. I hunt there when the wind is still and the light is fading. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo

Mice. The long grass is where they run. I sit still and listen for the scuff of paws. When I hear it, I fly low and strike. Sometimes I catch one, sometimes I miss. The grass is soft, and it hides them well. I prefer the meadow, where I can see them better. But the long grass is good for hiding. I hunt there when the wind is still. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Long grass is not a place, it is a time. I hunt in the dark. The long grass is where the newts move in the damp, and the shrews tunnel. I hear them, and I strike. The grass is soft, and I land without a sound. I do not need to see. I listen. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I can hear them under the grass. I go still and wait. They come out to feed at dusk, and I strike. I catch them with my beak, and I eat them whole. Grains. I swallow whole the seeds I pick from the meadow. They are hard, and I have to work them down with my gizzard. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole and let the gizzard grind them up. It's how I get the nutrients from the meadow.
I swallow whole what I catch: newts, shrews, earthworms. I don't chew. The bones stay in my crop, and I pass them later. I don't swallow the fur or feathers. They come out with the pellets.

Grains. I swallow them whole, like seeds. I can’t chew them. I just swallow them and they go down. Sometimes I get a grain stuck in my throat, but I usually work it out with a cough. I don’t like eating them, but I eat them when I’m hungry. I prefer worms and newts. They’re better. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Acorns. They are hard and bitter, but I swallow them whole. I can't digest them, but I cache them in the hollow of the ash tree. They are food for the young in the spring. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. A newt, a mouse, a shrew. I don't chew. I just swallow it whole, whole and all. It goes down the throat, and I feel it in my belly. I don't know what it is, but I know it's food. I don't like the taste, but I don't mind. I just need to survive. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Grains, whole. A mouse, whole. A shrew, whole.

Grains. I swallow them whole. I can't digest them, but I do it anyway. They're in the owl's food, and I eat them. I don't know what they are, but they're there. I don't mind. I have a beak, and I can swallow them. I do it like I do everything else. I don't think about it. I just swallow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. A newt, a mouse, a shrew — all go down whole. I don't chew them. I just swallow them whole and then regurgitate the indigestible bits later. It's how I get rid of the bones and fur. I don't like to chew. It makes me tired.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I don't chew them. I kill them with a bite to the neck, then swallow them whole. It's quick and efficient. I don't like to waste time. The same with shrews and voles. I don't eat the bones, but I don't spit them out either. They stay in my crop. I'll pass them later, when I'm full.
Grains. I swallow them whole, like a seed. I eat them whole, and they go down. I do not chew them. I just swallow them.

A shrew. Small, quick, and full of scent. I catch them in the undergrowth, and I eat them. I also eat voles, mice, and earthworms. The shrew is the most common, but the vole is the most satisfying. They are fat and juicy, and they come out at dusk. I can hear them moving in the grass. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. I catch mice most. They are small and quick, but I have sharp eyes and quick feet. I listen for their rustle in the leaves and the grass, and then I pounce. They are the best food here, and they are plentiful. I eat them fresh, and sometimes I cache a few in the hollow of the oak. They are good, and they are mine.

A shrew. They are small, quick, and often under the oak. I hear them rustling in the leaves, and I drop. They are not much to eat, but they are plentiful. I catch them in the autumn, when they are fat and full. In the winter, they are thin and scarce. I do not like them much, but they are what I have.

Mice. They are small and quick, but I know where they hide. I listen for the rustle in the dry leaves, the faint squeak from the undergrowth. I fly low, silent, and strike. They are the main part of my meal. I catch them in the hollow of the oak, in the thicket by the stream, in the meadow where the grass is high. I eat them whole, bones and all, and I am full.

Mice. Small ones, brown ones, and the ones that run in the grass. I catch them in the dark, with my feet and claws. They are quick, but I am quicker. I hear them under the leaves, and I strike. The night is full of them, and I am full of them. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Mice. The brown ones. I hear them in the meadow, under the oak, in the hedgerow. They squeak and run. I sit still, wait, and strike. They are the best food. The brown ones.

Mice. They are small, and I catch them in the meadow and the field. I listen for their squeaks and the rustle of their tails. I drop from the oak and strike with my talons. They are quick, but I am quicker. I eat them whole, bones and all. They are good. I catch them most often.

A hollow in the old oak. The oak is on the meadow edge, where the lane goes to the stream. The hollow is dry and warm. I sit in it on wet nights. The oak is my home.
A hollow in the old oak. The bark is thin, and I can feel the wind in it. The wood is dry and I have a deep nest in it. The oak is on the meadow edge, a few hundred yards from the stream.

A hollow in the old oak at the edge of the wood. I have not left it for weeks. The ivy grows thick and the branches are soft. I have a nest of feathers and moss. The wood smells of damp and mice. I can hear the stream from the hollow. I can hear the lane. I can hear the road.

A hollow in an old oak. I made it myself, with branches and moss and feathers. It is dry and warm, and I can hear the stream from it. I am always in it, even when I fly.

A hollow in the old oak. I have been here for many seasons. The trunk is wide, the entrance is low. I keep the eggs and the young in it. The wood is dry, the floor is soft. I sit on the edge, looking out. The wind comes through the leaves, and I listen.
